titre: Rites of Passage: One Three-Stage Pattern, Everywhere
accroche: In 1909, Arnold van Gennep spots the same three-stage construction in rites of birth, initiation, marriage, and funerals.
contenu_vulgarise:
On entering the army, recruits have their hair cut; at birth, the child is given a name. Nothing, apparently, connects these two gestures. In 1909, the French ethnologist and folklorist Arnold van Gennep published *Les rites de passage* (*The Rites of Passage*), in which he describes a three-stage construction found in ceremonies of all kinds.

## Separating, Suspending, Reintegrating

Van Gennep distinguishes rites of separation, rites of margin, and rites of incorporation. Rites of separation undo the old situation: he places there “all those in which something is cut,” such as the first haircut or the act of shaving the head. Next come rites of margin: a suspended time in which one is no longer what one was without yet being what one will become. Rites of incorporation, finally, install one in the new world: for birth, he cites the giving of a name and baptism.

These three groups do not carry the same weight everywhere. In his first chapter, he writes that rites of separation are more developed in funerals, rites of incorporation in marriage, and that rites of margin can form an important section in pregnancy, betrothal, or initiation. The chapter on funerals qualifies this: one would first expect rites of separation to occupy a central place, but the study of the facts shows the opposite. They are few and very simple there, the rites of margin sometimes long and complex, and it is those that incorporate the dead person into the world of the dead that are the most elaborate. He applies the scheme all the way down to the mere material passage, the door and the threshold, to which he devotes a chapter: rites performed on the threshold itself are rites of margin, preceded by purifications and followed by gestures of incorporation such as the presentation of salt or a shared meal. The sequence recurs in the rites of birth, puberty, betrothal, marriage, coronation, and funerals.

The word “liminal,” from the Latin *limen*, the threshold, comes from him: he proposes calling the rites of separation preliminal rites, those performed during the stage of margin liminal rites, and those of incorporation postliminal rites. It was Victor Turner who made it a central concept. In 1969, in *The Ritual Process*, the anthropologist, who had worked among the Ndembu of Zambia, took up and developed the notion of the liminal phase and associated with it communitas: a state without structure, in which the members of a group are equal, shared by those who go through a liminal phase together.

## What This Changes

The scheme ended up leaving the ground where van Gennep had found it. His table of contents already presents “pregnancy as a period of margin”: a state suspended between two stable positions, neither one nor the other, which has nothing of a religious ceremony. A structure first spotted in rites thus serves, from the very first book, to describe a state that has nothing of a ceremony, and the word “liminality” has stuck.

repere.texte: In Les rites de passage (1909), Arnold van Gennep describes three phases (separation, margin (liminal rites), incorporation) which he treats in connection with birth, puberty, initiation, coronation, betrothal, marriage, and funerals. In 1969, in The Ritual Process, Victor Turner develops the notion of the liminal phase and associates communitas with it, based on his study of the Ndembu of Zambia.
repere.source: Arnold van Gennep, Les rites de passage (The Rites of Passage), Paris, Émile Nourry, 1909; Victor Turner, The Ritual Process: Structure and Anti-Structure, 1969

carte.punch: Hair cut, a child named: the same three-stage pattern.
carte.idee: In 1909, Arnold van Gennep describes a three-stage pattern (separation, margin, incorporation) that he follows from the rites of birth to those of funerals. In 1969, Victor Turner develops the notion of the liminal phase, the one in the middle.

quiz.question: What does Victor Turner call “communitas” in 1969?
choix: The name van Gennep gave to the separation phase of the rite of passage
A ritual found only in societies without writing, according to Turner
The final ceremony that reintegrates the individual into the new status
The bond of equality between people who go through a liminal phase together
quiz.explication: Communitas is the state without structure, of equality among the members of a group, shared by those who live liminality, the phase of margin, together; it is neither the separation nor the incorporation described by van Gennep, nor a trait reserved for societies without writing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to chapter VIII of Les rites de passage, devoted to funerals, which rites are the most elaborate there?
choix: The rites of separation, which mark the break with the deceased
The rites of margin, during the period of suspension that precedes mourning
The rites of incorporation that bring the dead person into the world of the dead
None of the three groups of rites is especially developed in funerals
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Contrary to what one would expect, van Gennep shows in his chapter on funerals that rites of separation are few and simple there, while it is the rites incorporating the dead person into the world of the dead that are the most elaborate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the word “liminal,” which van Gennep introduces to name the rites of the margin phase, come from?
choix: From the Latin limen, meaning the threshold
From the Greek limne, meaning a lake or marshy area
From the name of a village where van Gennep observed a rite of passage
From a term borrowed directly from Victor Turner in 1969
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Van Gennep takes the word “liminal” from the Latin limen, the threshold, to name the rites performed during the stage of margin, between the preliminal rites of separation and the postliminal rites of incorporation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the anthropologist Victor Turner do in 1969, in The Ritual Process, drawing on his fieldwork among the Ndembu of Zambia?
choix: He rejects the notion of a liminal phase proposed by van Gennep as too vague
He invents van Gennep's three-stage scheme, which van Gennep had not yet formulated
He develops the notion of the liminal phase and associates communitas with it
He limits the use of van Gennep's scheme to funeral rites alone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Turner takes up and develops the notion of the liminal phase set out by van Gennep in 1909, and associates communitas with it, the state of equality without structure shared by those who go through it together.
